relations.note: Arash’s arrow fixes the boundary accepted in Afrasiyab’s peace settlement.
Afrāsyāb accepts Arash’s arrow-shot as the measure of Iran’s restored frontier.
Arash helps reverse Afrāsyāb’s conquest by recovering Iranian land.
After Bīžan’s liberation, Rostam’s party attacks Afrāsīāb’s palace or forces.
Afrāsīāb orders Bīžan arrested, condemns him, then imprisons him beneath Akvan’s stone.
Afrasiyab descends remotely from Fereydun through Tur.
Afrasiyab overruns Iran while Kay Kavus is captive in Hamavaran.
Afrasiyab repeatedly invades Kavus's realm and is ultimately defeated by Kavus's dynasty.
Kavus joins Kay Khosrow's ritual quest and celebrates Afrasiyab's capture and execution.
Afrasiyab is Kay Khosrow’s maternal grandfather through Farangis.
Young Kay Khosrow feigns simplicity when Afrasiyab tests him, escaping suspicion.
Kay Khosrow pursues his principal enemy through repeated campaigns.
Haosravah kills Afrasiyab to avenge Syāvaršan and Aγraēraθa.
Kay Khosrow executes Afrasiyab in vengeance for Siyavash and Aghrirath.
Haosrauuah kills him in vengeance for Siiāuuaršan and Aγraēraθa.
Kay Khosrow cuts the captured Afrasiyab in two despite passing compassion.
A variant brings Afrasiyab’s blood so Kay Khosrow can dip his hand.
Rostam helps Kay Ḵosrow overthrow Afrāsiāb and avenge Siāvash.

relations.myth: Rostam lifts Afrasiyab by his belt
relations.note: Rostam lifts Afrasiyab from his saddle, but Afrasiyab escapes when his belt breaks.
Rostam returns to occupied Iran and drives Afrasiyab’s forces out.
Rostam invades Turan, kills Sorkha, plunders Afrasiyab and rules there six years.
Rostam rescues Bijan from Afrasiyab’s pit and defeats the Turanian forces.
Rostam repeatedly fights and pursues the principal Turanian enemy.
In Šahmardān’s variant, Rostam helps procure Afrasiyab’s capture and urges his execution.
Afrasiyab initially receives the exiled Siyavash warmly and grants him land.
Siyavash concludes and honors a peace secured by hostages and gifts.
Afrasiyab becomes Siyavash’s father-in-law by giving him Farangis.
Siyavash commands Iranian forces against Afrasiyab before peace negotiations.
Afrasiyab orders Siyavash’s execution after accepting Garsivaz’s false accusations.
Early tradition holds Frangrasyan responsible for blood later avenged by Haosravah.
Afrasiyab receives Siyavash as a sonlike guest and grants him status.
Afrasiab provides Turanian troops for Sohrab's invasion of Iran.
Afrasiyab encourages Sohrab’s invasion while concealing Rostam’s identity from him.
Afrasiab secretly engineers non-recognition, hoping Sohrab and Rostam destroy each other.
Sorkha is Afrasiyab’s son.
Zal organizes resistance to Afrasiyab and advises subsequent Iranian campaigns.
Zāl clashes with Afrāsīāb and opposes his Turanian invasions.
The later genealogy makes Kaveh an ancestor of Bizhan through the Gudarzian line.
Bizhan revives the swooning king by sprinkling him with spring water.
Kay Khosrow locates Bīžan in Turan and commissions Rostam to rescue him.
Kay Khosrow locates the imprisoned Bizhan and dispatches Rostam to rescue him.
Bīžan serves Kay Khosrow, who accepts his offer to destroy Arman’s marauding boars.
Bīžan accompanies Kay Khosrow until the king’s disappearance and later dies returning through snow.
Bizhan accompanies Kay Khosrow toward disappearance and dies in Ferdowsi’s snowstorm.
Rostam is Bīžan’s maternal grandfather in the developed epic genealogy.
Rostam infiltrates Turan, removes Akvan’s stone, frees Bīžan, and commands the escape.
Rostam infiltrates Turan, removes the pit-stone, and brings Bižan home.
Esfandiyar fights Rostam after negotiations fail over Goshtasp's demand for chains.
Rostam shoots Esfandiyar through the eyes with the Simurgh-directed two-pointed arrow.
Using Simorḡ’s counsel, Rostam fatally shoots Esfandiyār in the eyes.
Dying, Esfandiyar exonerates Rostam and entrusts Bahman's education to him.
Some histories make Esfandiyar confront Rostam for rejecting Zoroaster's new religion.
Zal summons the Simurgh and helps devise the countermeasure that kills Esfandiyar.
Zal belongs to Rostam's household opposing Esfandiyar's attempt to impose chains.
Zāl tries preventing conflict but indirectly enables Esfandīār’s death.
Zāl directs mirror armor that reflects Simurgh’s light and dazzles Esfandīār.
Islamic-era genealogies derive Garšāsp from Ferēdūn’s son Tūz or Tūr.
Garšāsp acknowledges Fereydun’s sovereignty after Zahhāk is defeated.
Garšāsp pledges allegiance to Ferēdūn and delivers his captives.
Kərəsāspa receives the third portion of Glory after Fereydun receives the second.
Garšāsp ultimately kills the Dahāg whom Fereydun had bound.
Kāva raises the rebellion and leads the people to Fereydun.

relations.myth: Kaveh brings the uprising to Fereydun
relations.note: Kaveh leads the popular host to Fereydun and transfers leadership to the royal heir.
Fereydun enriches Kaveh’s leather apron with brocade, gold, jewels, and colored streamers.
Storyteller and oral traditions credit Kaveh with forging the weapon used by Fereydun.
Fereydun adopts Kāva’s leather apron as the Derafš-e Kāviān.
After refusing kingship, Kaveh selects Fereydun and serves as his commander and administrator.

relations.myth: Fereydun sends Kaveh to Khavar and Rum
relations.note: Kaveh campaigns as Fereydun’s general to impose royal authority and collect tribute.
The Oxus episode invokes Fereydun as Kay Khosrow’s ancestral precedent.
Their victories are linked typologically through the same transhistorical weapon.
Siyavash descends from Fereydun through his unnamed mother.
Rostam invokes Garšāsp or Karšāsb as an ancestor in his pedigree.
Modern comparativists treat Rostam as Garšāsp’s successor, replacement, or transformation.
New Persian epic places Zāl in the lineage descending from Garšāsp.
Gordafarid uses negotiation and attraction to escape, then mocks Sohrab from the wall.
Gordafarid challenges Sohrab, who overcomes her and exposes her identity.
Kavus worships and participates in the vengeance cycle beside his reigning grandson.
Kay Kavus is Kay Khosrow’s paternal grandfather.
Kay Khosrow is Kavus's grandson through Siyavash.
Kavus tests Kay Khosrow's succession claim and awards him the crown.
Kay Kavus tests his fitness for succession against Fariborz.
His unborn fravaši orders Nēryōsang to spare Kavus for salvation history.
Rostam repeatedly serves as Kavus's champion, defender, critic, and restorer of order.
Kavus quarrels with Rostam and rashly orders his execution before reconciliation.
Rostam completes the Seven Labors and frees the blinded, imprisoned Kavus.
Rostam captures Šambarān and liberates Kay Us and the deported Iranians.
Rostam defeats Hamavaran's allies and compels Kavus's captors to release him.
Rostam rescues the blinded and imprisoned king from Māzandarān’s demons.
Rostam rescues Kay Kāvus from captivity in Hāmāvarān.
Rostam rescues Kay Kāvus after the king’s flying-throne disaster.
Rostam repeatedly defends and admonishes the impulsive king.
Kavus accepts Siyavash's ordeal by fire as proof against Sudabeh's accusation.
Kavus judges Sudabeh’s accusation and witnesses Siyavash’s vindication by fire.
Siyavash is Kavus's son and heir across Middle Persian and epic traditions.
Kavus demands treaty-breaking, making Siyavash's return impossible and precipitating his exile.
Kavus orders Siyavash to violate his treaty, driving him into exile.
Sohrab invades Iran intending to depose Kavus and enthrone Rostam.
Sohrab invades intending to depose Kavus and challenges his royal authority.
Kavus deliberately withholds healing medicine after Sohrab is mortally wounded.
Kavus denies or delays healing medicine because he fears Sohrab united with Rostam.
Zal warns Kavus, receives his appeal for aid, and dispatches Rostam.
Zāl and his heroic house repeatedly rescue Kay Kāvus’s monarchy.
Zāl serves Kay Kāvus as elder counselor and supports his monarchy.
Rostam champions his cause and leads campaigns against Turanian forces.
Rostam supports Kay Ḵosrow’s kingship and campaigns of vengeance.
Kay Khosrow sends Rostam to rescue Bizhan after locating him.
Siiāuuaršan is Kay Khosrow’s father in Avestan and later traditions.
Kay Khosrow wages war and kills Afrasiyab to avenge his father.
Zāl opposes Kay Khosrow’s chosen successor until the king establishes Lohrāsp’s fitness.
Zāl disputes Kay Ḵosrow’s nomination of Lohrāsp but accepts the royal order.
Rostam campaigns against Turan to avenge Siāvash’s execution.
Rostam accompanies Siyavash during his successful command against Afrasiyab.
Rostam mourns Siyavash, kills Sudabeh, and invades Turan in retaliation.
Rostam trains and protects the young prince.
Rostam fosters Siyavash and teaches him warfare, justice, speech, and kingship.
Rostam denies his identity and invents a rule after losing their first bout.
Rostam falsely claims Iranian custom requires two falls before killing a champion.
Father and unrecognized son meet in two wrestling combats.
They fight anonymously with multiple weapons, without a decisive result.
Sohrab throws Rostam in wrestling but accepts his plea and spares him.
Rostam mortally stabs Sohrāb before recognizing him by the token.
Rostam throws Sohrab and mortally wounds him with a dagger.
Sohrāb is Rostam’s son by Tahmina.
Zāl is Rostam’s father.
Zāl summons the Simurgh to heal the wounded Rostam and Raḵš.
Zāl counsels restraint before helping Rostam learn Esfandīār’s vulnerability.
Sohrab is Rudabeh's paternal grandson.
Rudabeh participates in family mourning for Sohrab in received versions.
Sohrab is Zal's paternal grandson.
Zal receives the dead youth within the mourning Sistanian family.

god_relations.note: Ahura Mazda opposes Afrasiyab’s threat to corrupt grain and drink.
Ohrmazd reverses the immortality that Ahriman had intended for Afrasiyab.
Ahriman originally makes Afrasiyab immortal before Ohrmazd alters his condition.
Middle Persian theology classifies Afrasiyab among Ahriman’s destructive instruments.
Afrasiyab sacrifices lavishly to Anāhitā, but she refuses his request for glory.
The Avestan deity binds Afrasiyab and delivers him to Kavi Haosravah.

god_relations.myth: Capture at Hang and Lake Čēčast
god_relations.note: Hom captures Afrasiyab near his cave and helps expose him at the lake.
The earth goddess is described as Afrasiyab’s wife or violated partner.
Esfandarmad orders the boundary bow and arrow that curtail Afrasiyab’s dominion.
Tishtrya’s celestial speed is compared to Arash’s proverbial arrow.

god_relations.myth: Divine wind carries the boundary arrow
god_relations.note: God orders the wind to carry Arash’s arrow toward Iran’s frontier.
Bahram finds or visits the primordial king’s treasure; they never meet.
Esfandiyar belongs to the righteous Zoroastrian community; no direct dialogue survives.
The beneficent Simurgh reveals Esfandiyar's vulnerable eyes and directs the fatal weapon.
Reflected Simurgh radiance dazzles Esfandiyar until he imagines his eyes pierced.
Middle Persian and epic genealogies make Fereydun a descendant of Yima.
Haoma recounts how Āθβiia’s pressing was rewarded by Fereydun’s birth.
Fereydun defeats the three-headed being created by Angra Mainyu.
The Avestan tradition says Fereydun smote Dahāka and explicitly recalls his killing.
Later tradition has Fereydun bind and imprison Dahāg instead of killing him.
Fereydun strikes Zahhāk with the ox-headed mace before imprisoning him.
Ahriman makes the initially immortal Fereydun mortal.
After receiving Fereydun’s sacrifice, Anāhitā grants victory and the captives’ release.
The second portion of Yima’s departed Glory adheres to Fereydun.
Fereydun receives the second portion of the Glory that departed Yima.
Middle Persian tradition presents Fereydun as the avenger of Yima.
Mithra receives the first portion of Glory before Fereydun receives the second.
Ohrmazd commands Fereydun not to kill Dahāg, preventing demonic creatures’ release.
Haoma rewards Θrita’s sacrifice with Kərəsāspa and his brother.
Kərəsāspa receives the third portion of Yima’s departed royal Glory.
New Persian traditions make Garšāsp a descendant or seed of Jamšid.
Mithra receives the first share of Glory and Kərəsāspa the third.
Anāhitā accepts Kərəsāspa’s sacrifice and grants his requested victory.
Ohrmazd judges Karsāsp and recognizes that his victories preserved creation.
Ohrmazd orders Karsāsp awakened to kill the escaped Dahāg.
Karsāsp injures or extinguishes sacred Fire when the serpent overturns his pot.
Fire accuses Karsāsp and initially refuses him admission to paradise.

god_relations.myth: Dahāg escapes at the end time
god_relations.note: The awakened Karsāsp kills the escaped Dahāg with his club.

god_relations.myth: Dahāg offers conversion and joint rule
god_relations.note: Karsāsp strikes Dahāg after his belated acceptance comes too late.
In a Persian variant, Dahāg accepts Karsāsp’s offer and evil departs.
Żaḥḥāk challenges Garšāsp to slay a dragon and commands his Indian campaign.
Sōšāns forces or persuades Sām to accept the religion before fighting Dahāg.

god_relations.myth: Kaveh confronts Zahhak and begins the revolt
god_relations.note: Kaveh recovers his son, tears Zahhak’s testimonial, denounces the court, and rallies a revolt.
Kaveh defeats Zahhak’s forces and joins Fereydun in defeating or killing the tyrant.
Some oral accounts make Kaveh capture, torture, kill, or continually guard Zahhak.

god_relations.myth: Kawa kills Dehak and signals liberation
god_relations.note: Modern Kurdish tradition makes Kawa kill Dehak with a hammer and light liberation fires.

god_relations.myth: Jamshid reveals Fereydun in Kaveh’s dream
god_relations.note: In folk versions Jamshid appears in a dream and reveals Fereydun’s location to Kaveh.
Kavus sacrifices to her, and she grants his request for sovereignty.
Ohrmazd recalls the Kavian glory, causing Kavus and his army to fall.
His glory, victories, and future service belong to Mazdean sacred order.
Haoma captures Fraŋrasiiān and delivers him bound to Kay Khosrow.
Hōm captures and binds Afrasiyab before bringing him for execution.
Aži Dahāka’s defeat is typologically linked to Haosrauuah’s victorious weapon.
Medieval literature conflates Kay Khosrow’s cup with Jamshid’s world-revealing cup.
Rostam descends maternally from Żaḥḥāk through Mehrāb and Rudāba.
Rudabeh is his remote descendant; this lineage threatens her marriage to Zāl.
Siyavash rides through blazing piles unharmed, publicly proving his innocence.
Siyavash belongs to the Kayanian sequence associated with the royal Glory.

god_relations.myth: Zāl’s exposure and fosterage on Alborz
god_relations.note: She rescues the exposed infant, feeds him, and raises him.

god_relations.myth: Zāl’s return from the Simurgh’s nest
god_relations.note: She gives Zāl feathers through which he can summon her.
She instructs Zāl how to deliver Rostam and heal Rudāba.
She teaches Zāl and Rostam how Esfandīār can be defeated.

*Nōhīn.note: The Turk Nōhīn shoots Karsāsp while the hero sleeps.

Abraham.note: Al-Maqdisī compares or identifies Fereydun with Abraham.

Abīweh.note: The Dēnkard names Kavus as Abīweh's eldest son.
Several chronicle genealogies place Abīweh as an intermediary ancestor rather than father.

Aghrirath.note: Afrasiyab kills Aghrirath for helping captive Iranian warriors escape.

Ahrimen.note: Dahāg urges Sām to serve Ahrimen, but Sām refuses and curses him.

Akvan Div.note: Bīžan is imprisoned beneath a stone formerly hurled by Akvan, but they never meet.
Akvan abducts Rostam and tries to reverse his requested destination.
After surviving the sea, Rostam recovers Rakhsh and kills Akvan.

Alexander.note: Later synchronism connects their wisdom quests, cups, caves, and vanished-king traditions.

Alp Ariz.note: Alp Ariz is Afrasiyab’s gigantic son in Oghuz fragments.

Alvāy.note: The Sistanian warrior fights Esfandiyar's forces and is killed by Nush-Azar.

Andariman.note: Esfandiyar captures and hangs Arjasp's kinsman or commander Andariman.

Ard Wahišt.note: Fire’s guardian accuses Garšāsp but pardons him in one Persian account.

Ardashir.note: Ardashir is named as Esfandiyar's brother in canonical epic genealogy.

Arjasp.note: Esfandiyar defeats Arjasp's anti-Zoroastrian forces after Zarer's death.
Released from prison, Esfandiyar defeats Arjasp's invading field army.
Disguised as a merchant, Esfandiyar enters Arjasp's fortress with concealed warriors.
Esfandiyar kills Arjasp in his private quarters after infiltrating the fortress.

Arnavāz.note: Fereydun asks for and accomplishes her release from Dahāka.
A widespread later tradition makes the rescued Arnavāz Fereydun’s consort.

Arzhang Div.note: Arzhang serves the demonic power holding Kavus and dies during Rostam's rescue.

Aršak.note: Modern scholarship hypothetically identifies or links Arash with the Arsacid ancestral figure.
Aršak.source: Modern reconstruction from names and coins

Aržang Div.note: Rostam assaults Aržang Div’s camp and kills him.

Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā.note: He sacrifices for victory, and she grants his request.

Arəzošamana.note: Kərəsāspa kills the strong heroic adversary Arəzošamana.

Astuuat̰.ərəta.note: The future savior inherits the weapon associated with Haosrauuah’s victory.
Kay Husrōy assists the future savior’s Renovation.

Auruuasāra.note: Auruuasāra seeks divine aid to overtake or defeat Haosrauuah.

Aēšma.note: Aēšma inflames Kavus's ambition and induces his attempted conquest of heaven.

Aŋra Mainiiu.note: Kərəsāspa prevents Snāuuiδka from harnessing Aŋra Mainiiu to his chariot.

Aši.note: He petitions her for victory and vengeance for Siiāuuaršan and Aγraēraθa.

Aškbus.note: Fighting on foot, Rostam kills the mounted Aškbus with an arrow.

Aγraēraθa.note: Kay Khosrow avenges Aγraēraθa’s killing alongside his father’s death.

Bahman.note: Esfandiyar is Bahman's father in Middle Persian and epic genealogy.
Canonical and historical traditions retain Bahman as Esfandiyar's son and successor.
Esfandiyar entrusts Bahman to Rostam for education while dying.
The dying Esfandiyār entrusts Bahman to Rostam’s care.
Bahman later attacks Rostam’s household and ancestral realm.
A chronicle variant makes Bahman kill Rostam and members of his house.
Bahman confiscates Zāl’s wealth and imprisons him before releasing him.
Early historical versions say Bahman kills Zāl.
The lost verse epic reportedly says Bahman kills Zāl.
Zāl resists Bahman, who captures and later releases him.

Bahram.note: Siyavash entrusts the Iranian army to Bahram until Tus arrives.

Bahrām.note: Bahrām is Bīžan’s paternal uncle and a member of the same heroic clan.

Bahū.note: Garšāsp defeats the Indian usurper Bahū and restores the displaced king.

Barman.note: Afrasiyab assigns Barman to accompany Sohrab and conceal his parentage.
Barman supports and supervises Sohrab's expedition under Afrasiab's orders.
Barman helps execute the plan preventing Sohrab from recognizing Rostam.

Barmāya.note: The miraculous multicolored cow nurses Fereydun for three years.
A companion named Barmāya accompanies Fereydun in textually variable accounts.

Barmāyūn.note: The Middle Persian genealogy names Barmāyūn as Frēdōn’s brother.

Bastwar.note: The cousins fight to avenge Zarer, with variant credit for killing Wīdrafš.

Behāfarid.note: Behāfarid is Esfandiyar's sister in the canonical epic.
Her possible wife-sister status is a modern reconstruction, not explicit narration.
Esfandiyar frees Behāfarid after Arjasp abducts and confines her.

Benjamin.note: Mirḵᵛānd makes Garšāsp’s mother a descendant of Benjamin.

Bijan.note: Afrasiyab condemns Bijan to death, then substitutes imprisonment in a pit.

Borzu.note: Kavus and the Iranian nobles pardon Borzu after learning he descends from Sohrab.
Kay Khosrow and the Iranian army come to Borzu’s aid.
Kay Khosrow rewards Borzu with Ghur and Herat.
Borzu is Rostam’s grandson through Sohrāb.
Borzu fights his unrecognized grandfather before their kinship is discovered.
The later epic cycle makes Borzu the son of Sohrab and Shahru.

Borzū.note: Afrasiyab recruits Borzu and directs him against Iran before his ancestry is revealed.
Borzū, Sohrāb’s son, is a later-cycle descendant of Zāl.
Zāl appears as senior patriarch within Borzū’s heroic family cycle.

Bānu Gošasp.note: Bānu Gošasp is Bīžan’s mother in the developed epic genealogy.
Bānu Gošasp is Rostam’s warrior daughter in the secondary cycle.

Bānū Gošasp.note: Bānū Gošasp is Rostam’s daughter and Zāl’s granddaughter.
Bahman captures her with Zāl, and both are eventually freed.

Bārmān.note: Bārmān supports Sohrāb’s invasion and helps prevent father-son recognition.

Būšāsp.note: The demoness Būšāsp overcomes Karsāsp with sleep after Nōhīn shoots him.

Druuāspā.note: He sacrifices to her for the power to kill Fraŋrasiiān.

Drvāspā.note: Drvāspā grants Haoma and Haosravah power to bind and kill Afrasiyab.

Dāštayāna.note: Kərəsāspa kills the brood of Dāštayāna.

Eblis.note: Eblis tempts Kavus to seek heaven's dominion and precipitates his disastrous flight.

Espanuy.note: Bīžan captures Espanuy, a woman associated with Tezhav’s household.

Eṯreṭ.note: Asadi places Eṯreṭ as Garšāsp’s father in a different genealogy.

Faramarz.note: Kavus commissions Faramarz to aid Nowshad Shah in India.

Farangis.note: Farangis is Afrasiyab’s daughter and mother of Kay Khosrow.
Afrasiyab gives Farangis in marriage to the exiled Siyavash.
Afrasiyab orders pregnant Farangis killed or beaten until she miscarries.
Kavus welcomes Siyavash's widow and the mother of his grandson Kay Khosrow.
Farangis is his mother in Ferdowsi’s genealogy.
Mother and son flee Turan and cross the Oxus together.
Siyavash marries Afrasiyab’s daughter Farangis, mother of Kay Khosrow.
Farangis pleads for Siyavash, mourns him, and condemns her father afterward.

Fariborz.note: Bīžan restores the Kāvīānī banner after Fariborz retreats with or abandons it.
Fariborz is Kavus's son and a candidate to inherit the throne.
Kavus tests Fariborz's succession claim; Fariborz fails to capture the fortress.
Kay Khosrow defeats the rival claimant by taking the demon-held fortress.
After losing the succession contest, Fariborz serves Kay Khosrow.
Fariborz accompanies Kay Khosrow and dies in the snowstorm.

Farshidvard.note: Farshidvard is Esfandiyar's beloved brother in the canonical epic.
News of Farshidvard's mortal wounds persuades Esfandiyar to fight Arjasp again.

Farāmarz.note: Farāmarz captures Borzu and thereby frustrates Afrasiyab’s plan against Iran.
Bīžan appears with Farāmarz in later epic tradition; their precise relationship varies by recension.
Farāmarz fights beside Rostam’s faction and attacks Esfandiyār’s camp.
Farāmarz avenges Rostam by destroying Kabul and executing its king.
Farāmarz is Rostam’s son and Zāl’s grandson.
Zāl acts as elder patriarch and correspondent during Farāmarz’s adventures.

Farānak.note: Farānak is Fereydun’s mother and protects him from Zahhāk.

Ferud.note: Bīžan fights Ferud, the son of Siyavash, during the Iranian campaign.

Forud.note: Forud is Kay Khosrow’s paternal half-brother through Siyavash.
Kay Khosrow orders Forud protected, but Tus’s army kills him.

Frash-ham-vareta.note: Frash-ham-vareta is named among Esfandiyar's brothers in early tradition.

Frashō.kara.note: Frashō.kara is named among Esfandiyar's brothers in early tradition.

Gandarw.note: Gandarw drags Karsāsp into the sea before Karsāsp binds and overcomes him.

Garsivaz.note: Garsivaz instigates Siyavash’s murder and remains Afrasiyab’s accomplice.
Garsivaz leads armed men who overwhelm, bind, and arrest Bīžan in Manīža’s palace.
Garsivaz engineers Siyavash's death and later enters Kavus's dynastic vengeance narrative.
Garsivaz slanders Siyavash to Afrasiyab and misrepresents Afrasiyab to Siyavash.
Garsivaz’s deception instigates the capture and execution of Siyavash.

Gaṇdərəβa.note: Kərəsāspa defeats the golden-heeled sea monster after seeking divine aid.

Giv.myth: Escape of Kay Khosrow and Farangis
Giv.note: Giv penetrates Afrasiyab’s realm and escapes with Kay Khosrow and Farangis.
Giv is presented as Kaveh’s descendant through the Gudarzian genealogical line.
Kavus orders Tus to hang Giv alongside Rostam, though the order is not executed.
Giv retrieves Kay Khosrow and Farangis from Turan and presents them to Kavus.
Rostam is Giv’s fellow champion and rescues his son Bižan.

Giv.myth: Discovery and rescue of Siyavash’s family
Giv.note: Giv finds Siyavash’s mother, then later escorts his widow and son.

God.note: Bīžan prays to God while in distress, without a narrated divine appearance or direct oracle.
Rostam repeatedly prays to, thanks, and invokes God.

Godarz.note: Godarz receives Soruš’s dream and sends Gēv to find Kay Khosrow.
Godarz commands Kay Khosrow’s armies and kills Pirān.

Gorgin.note: Kay Khosrow judges Gorgin for abandoning Bizhan in the pit.

Gorgin son of Milād.note: Gorgin lures Bīžan toward Manīža’s encampment and later lies about his disappearance.
Gorgin later accompanies the expedition sent to rescue Bīžan.

Gorgsar.note: The captured enemy commander is coerced into guiding Esfandiyar toward the fortress.
Esfandiyar kills Gorgsar after repeatedly questioning him and receiving a hostile answer.

Goruy.note: Goruy obeys Afrasiyab’s order and cuts Siyavash’s throat.
Goruy or Kidar executes or assists in killing Kavus's son Siyavash.
Kay Khosrow has Goruy quartered, beheaded, and cast into water.
Kay Khosrow orders or personally carries out Goruy’s brutal execution.

Goshtasp.note: The canonical epic identifies Goshtasp as Esfandiyar's father.
Esfandiyar champions his father's kingdom and religion after being promised the throne.
Goshtasp humiliates, chains, and imprisons Esfandiyar after Korazm's accusation.
Goshtasp repeatedly promises the crown, then knowingly sends Esfandiyar against Rostam.

Gostaham.note: Gostaham fights with Bīžan among the Iranian champions.
Gostaham accompanies Bīžan during Kay Khosrow’s final journey.
Gostaham accompanies Kay Khosrow and dies in the snow after his disappearance.

Gostahm.note: Zāl rejects Gostahm as unsuitable to succeed Nowḏar.

Gozhdaham.note: Gozhdaham evacuates his garrison after Gordafarid delays Sohrab's assault.

Goštāsp.note: Rostam acknowledges the king but refuses Goštāsp’s humiliating demand for bonds.
Zāl hosts and shelters the displaced Goštāsp for two years.
A learned tradition claims Zāl wrote books maligning Goštāsp.

Gudarz.note: Gudarz commands against Afrasiyab, and his house destroys much of the Turanian clan.
Later epic genealogy traces Gudarz’s lineage back to Kaveh through Qaren and Kashvad.
Gudarz serves Kavus as senior counsellor and commander and supports Kay Khosrow.
Gudarz serves alongside Rostam as an elder Iranian champion.
Gudarz unsuccessfully requests Kavus's healing remedy for the mortally wounded Sohrab.

Guruy.note: Guruy cuts Siyavash’s throat or beheads him on Afrasiyab’s order.

Gēv.note: Gēv finds Kay Khosrow and escorts him and Farangis to Iran.
Gēv accompanies Kay Khosrow during the divinely assisted conquest.
Gēv receives and executes commands during Kay Khosrow’s reign.
Gēv accompanies the departing king and dies in the ensuing snowstorm.

Gīv.note: Gīv mourns and searches for Bīžan, petitions Kay Khosrow, and receives him after his rescue.

Gōdarz.note: Gōdarz is Bīžan’s paternal grandfather and head of his warrior house.
Bīžan fights beside Gōdarz or within the same Iranian host.
Zāl retrieves Gōdarz’s corpse and gives him a splendid burial.

Gōšurūn.note: Gōšurūn prevents Karsāsp’s return to hell because he protected animal creation.

Hitāspa.note: Kərəsāspa kills his brother’s murderer and drags him behind a chariot.

Hojir.note: Sohrab defeats and captures the Iranian champion at the White Fortress.
Hojir identifies other Iranian warriors but deliberately conceals Rostam.

Homan.note: Homan accompanies Sohrab as commander and field adviser.
Knowing Afrasiab's plan, Homan denies or obscures Rostam's identity.

Homay.note: Homay is Esfandiyar's sister in the canonical epic.
Goshtasp explicitly awards Homay to Esfandiyar as wife after his victory.
Esfandiyar frees Homay after Arjasp abducts and confines her.

Hostile Simurgh.note: Esfandiyar kills the hostile monstrous bird using a fortified battle device.

Hum.note: Hum captures Afrasiyab and brings him into Kay Khosrow and Kavus's vengeance cycle.

Human.note: Afrasiyab assigns Human to accompany Sohrab and conceal his parentage.

Hutaosā.note: Hutaosā or Hutos is Esfandiyar's mother in early and Middle Persian genealogy.

Hōmān.note: The Turanian commander Hōmān fights Rostam.
Hōmān helps conceal Rostam’s identity from Sohrāb.

Hūmān.note: Bīžan faces Hūmān in single combat during the Twelve Combats.
Bīžan kills Hūmān, Piran’s brother, in single combat.

Imam ʿAli.note: Shiʿi storytelling compares or assimilates Rostam’s champion qualities to Imam ʿAli.

Iraj.note: Iraj is Fereydun’s favored youngest son.
Fereydun grants Iraj Iran, the throne, and royal insignia.

Jahāngir.note: Jahāngir is Rostam’s son in a later secondary epic.
Jahāngir encounters his father without recognition, repeating the kin-combat motif.

Jamasp.note: The royal sage foretells that Esfandiyar will die at Rostam's hand.
Jamasp asks the imprisoned prince to return and save the kingdom.
Jamasp and Esfandiyar accompany Goshtasp in the fire miracle.

Jarira.note: Jarira is the mother of Kay Khosrow’s half-brother Forud.
Siyavash marries Piran’s daughter Jarira, who bears Farud.

Kamak.note: Karsāsp kills or neutralizes the immense bird whose wings block rain.

Kamangir.note: Kamangir appears among warriors or affiliated champions under Afrasiyab’s kingship.

Karakhan.note: Karakhan appears as Afrasiyab’s son in extended Turanian genealogy.

Kashvad.note: The stable later genealogy makes Kashvad Kaveh’s grandson through Qaren.
A Kurdish verse Shahnameh summary instead names Kashvad directly as Kaveh’s son.
Kashvad.source: Kurdish verse tradition collected by Enjavi

Katayun.note: Canonical tradition makes Katayun, princess of Rum, Esfandiyar's mother.
Katayun warns Esfandiyar that Goshtasp intends his death and later mourns him.

Katāyūn.note: The Middle Persian genealogy names Katāyūn as Frēdōn’s brother.

Kavi Xvarənah.note: The royal Glory cleaves to Kərəsāspa and empowers his heroic strength.

Kay Husrōy.note: Sām temporarily rules seven continents, then transfers sovereignty to Kay Husrōy.
Kay Husrōy.source: Māh ī Frawardīn Rōz ī Hordad 31

Kay Husrōy.note: Kay Husrōy passes the undead Karsāsp and witnesses his religious profession.

Kay Qobad.note: Kay Qobad is raised as king and checks Afrasiyab with Rostam’s aid.
Ferdowsi makes Kay Kavus the direct son and successor of Kay Qobad.
Some Pahlavi and chronicle genealogies make Kay Qobad a more remote ancestor.

Kay Qobād.note: Rostam retrieves Kay Qobād from Alborz and defeats his enemies.
Rostam establishes Kay Qobād as Iran’s king.
Zāl identifies Kay Qobād as rightful king and offers him the crown.
Zāl sends Rostam to fetch Kay Qobād from Alborz.

Keresavazda.note: Keresavazda is Afrasiyab’s brother or close kinsman.

Khiżr.note: Later wonder lore associates both with water, immortality, cups, and vanished kings.

King of Hamavaran.note: Kavus's father-in-law betrays and imprisons him despite Sudabeh's warning.
Kavus campaigns against Hamavaran before demanding the king's daughter in marriage.

King of Kabul.note: The king conspires with Shaghad to lure Rostam onto the trapped hunting ground.

King of Mazandaran.note: Kavus invades his country and later challenges and defeats his forces.

King of Samangan.note: Sohrab is the unnamed king of Samangan's maternal grandson.
The king supports or permits his grandson's military mobilization.

King of Samangān.note: The king hosts Rostam, recovers Rakhsh, and accepts Tahmina’s union.

Kiyānuš.note: Kiyānuš accompanies Fereydun as a companion or brother-in-arms.

Kohram.note: Esfandiyar captures and executes Arjasp's son or commander Kohram.

Korazm.note: Korazm falsely accuses Esfandiyar of planning to depose Goshtasp.

Kāren.note: Later tradition makes Kāren and Arash collaborating champions of Manūčehr.

Kāvya Uśanas.note: Modern scholars compare or identify him with Kavus; no ancient encounter is attested.

Kūrang.note: A Sistanian variant sometimes makes Kūrang Garšāsp’s son.
Asadi makes Kūrang an ancestor who receives Jamšid’s fugitive son.

Kərəsauuazda.note: Haosrauuah binds Kərəsauuazda together with Fraŋrasiiān.
Kay Khosrow has Garsivaz tortured so his cries expose Afrasiyab.

Lohrasp.note: Lohrasp is Esfandiyar's grandfather in the Kayanian genealogy.
Esfandiyar avenges his grandfather's killing by Arjasp's invading forces.

Lohrāsp.note: Kay Khosrow grants Lohrāsp the kingship despite noble resistance.
Zāl initially opposes Lohrāsp’s designation as royal heir.

Malek Ṭāwus.note: A regional theological scheme treats Rostam as a manifestation of Malek Ṭāwus.
Some Malek Ṭāwusi groups treat Zāl as a manifestation of Malek Ṭāwus.

Manijeh.note: Manijeh is Afrasiyab’s daughter and Bijan’s eventual wife.
Afrasiyab disowns Manijeh and leaves her destitute for protecting Bijan.

Maniža.note: Maniža helps the disguised Rostam locate and rescue Bižan.

Manuchehr.note: Middle Persian and historical versions make Afrasiyab besiege or displace Manuchehr.
Manuchehr descends from Fereydun through Iraj’s surviving line.
Fereydun raises or conceals Manuchehr, recognizes him, and commissions Iraj’s vengeance.

Manūčehr.note: Arash and Manūčehr jointly recover Iranian land from Afrāsyāb.
Arash acts as Manūčehr’s chosen archer in the territorial settlement.
Manūčehr tests and invests Zāl, then authorizes his marriage.

Mehrnush.note: Mehrnush is Esfandiyar's son in canonical epic genealogy.
Mehrnush accompanies his father during the fatal expedition and is killed.

Mehrnuš.note: Rostam’s son Farāmarz kills Mehrnuš during the surrounding battle.

Mehrāb.note: Mehrāb of Kabul is Rostam’s maternal grandfather.
Mehrāb hosts Zāl, becomes his father-in-law, and receives his protection.

Mihr-tirs.note: The Bundahišn names Mihr-tirs as a son of Esfandiyar.

Narimān.note: Narimān is an ancestor in Rostam’s Sistanian paternal line.

Narēmān.note: Narēmān campaigns with Garšāsp under Fereydun’s overlordship.
Garšāsp adopts his nephew Narēmān, establishing the later heroic lineage.

Narīmān.note: The Sistanian genealogy makes Narīmān Garšāsp’s grandson.
The Mojmal genealogy makes Narīmān Garšāsp’s direct son.
Narīmān is Zāl’s grandfather in the Sistanian heroic genealogy.

Nivika.note: Kərəsāspa kills the brood of Nivika.

Noah.note: Al-Bīrūnī reports a learned equation of Fereydun with Noah.

Nowshad Shah.note: Kavus sends Nowshad Shah military aid through Faramarz.

Nowzar.note: Afrasiyab defeats, captures and personally beheads Nowzar.
Other traditions place Nowzar’s death during Afrasiyab’s attack on Manuchehr.

Nowḏar.note: Zāl serves during Nowḏar’s reign and intervenes after his murder.

Nush-Azar.note: Nush-Azar is Esfandiyar's son in canonical epic genealogy.
Nush-Azar fights beside Esfandiyar, kills Alvāy, and is killed by Zavara.

Nēryōsang.note: Nēryōsang accompanies Srōš when Karsāsp is awakened to fight Dahāg.
Nēryōsang pursues the falling Kavus to kill him but ultimately spares him.

Olād.note: Rostam defeats Olād and spares him in exchange for guidance.
The defeated Olād guides Rostam through Māzandarān.

Pashang.note: Pashang is unanimously Afrasiyab’s father in the developed tradition.
Afrasiyab invades Iran after Pashang commands him to exploit its disorder.

Pashotan.note: Pashotan is Esfandiyar's brother in Zoroastrian and epic traditions.
Pashotan counsels Esfandiyar, accompanies his expeditions, and attacks the fortress.

Pathana.note: Kərəsāspa kills all nine members of Pathana’s brood.

Pašutan.note: Pašutan later saves Rostam’s father Zāl from Bahman.

Pašōtan.note: Pašōtan intercedes with Bahman and secures Zāl’s release.

Peshotan.note: Peshotan later inhabits or emerges from Kangdiz, the fortress Siyavash built.

Pilsam.note: Pilsam serves Afrasiyab as a Turanian champion and fights the Iranians.

Piran.note: Piran is Afrasiyab’s uncle in Ferdowsi, though other genealogies vary.
Piran serves as counselor and general while repeatedly restraining Afrasiyab’s violence.
Rostam encounters Piran as a respected Turanian opponent.

Piran Viseh.note: Piran welcomes Siyavash, supports him at court, and arranges his marriages.
Piran pleads for Siyavash’s life but cannot prevent his execution.

Piran son of Viseh.note: Piran persuades Afrāsīāb not to execute Bīžan, saving him from immediate death.

Pirān.note: Pirān protects Siyavash, Farangis, and Kay Khosrow, indirectly preserving Kavus's dynasty.
Pirān protects and raises him in Turan, concealing him from Afrasiyab.
Pirān later commands Turanian forces against Kay Khosrow’s armies.
Kay Khosrow mourns Pirān after Godarz kills his former protector.

Pitaona.note: Kərəsāspa kills Pitaona while he is attended by many pairikās.

Pulādvand.note: Rostam wrestles Pulādvand but cannot decisively overcome his magical protection.

Pūrtōrā Āspiyān.note: Middle Persian genealogy names Pūrtōrā Āspiyān as Frēdōn’s father.

Qaren.note: Qaren is named as Kaveh’s son and becomes a later hero and commander.

Qaz.note: Qaz is Afrasiyab’s daughter in Kāšḡarī’s geographical legends.

Qobad.note: Qobad is named as Kaveh’s son in the later epic tradition.
Kaveh tries to kill his son for insulting royal authority, but relatives intervene.

Rakhsh.note: Manīža’s inquiry about Rostam’s horse Rakhsh helps test the disguised rescuer’s identity.
Esfandiyar severely wounds Rostam's heroic horse during their battle.
Rakhsh carries Rostam through the journey undertaken to rescue Kavus.
Rakhsh is Rostam’s chosen mount, warning companion, rescuer, and fellow combatant.
Rakhsh falls into the concealed pit and dies beside Rostam.

Rohām.note: Rohām belongs to Rostam’s selected party or associated force during Bīžan’s rescue.

Rudāba.note: They court one another and marry despite dynastic opposition.
Zāl summons the Simurgh, whose instructions save Rudāba during childbirth.

Rūyīn.note: Bīžan fights Rūyīn, the son of Piran, during the Iran–Turan wars.

Salm.note: Fereydun grants Salm Rūm and the western lands.

Satan.note: Satan gives Afrasiyab a magical belt in a poem unrelated to the established cycle.
Satan convinces Kavus that he is divine and should ascend toward heaven.

Shaghad.note: Shaghad engineers the concealed spear-pit that mortally wounds Rostam.
Dying, Rostam shoots through a plane tree and kills Shaghad.

Shahriyar.note: Later epic genealogy makes Sohrab Shahriyar's great-grandfather through Borzu.

Shahrnāz.note: Fereydun asks for and accomplishes her release from Dahāka.
A widespread later tradition makes the rescued Shahrnāz Fereydun’s consort.

Shedasp.note: Shedasp is named as Esfandiyar's brother in canonical epic genealogy.

Shida.note: Afrasiyab’s son challenges Kay Khosrow to a duel.
Kay Khosrow kills Shida in single combat.

Shideh.note: Shideh is Afrasiyab’s son and champion.
Afrasiyab sends Shideh into single combat, where Kay Khosrow kills him.

Simorḡ.note: Simorḡ directs the procedure that saves Rudāba and delivers Rostam.
Simorḡ heals the gravely wounded Rostam and Rakhsh.
Simorḡ reveals Esfandiyār’s vulnerable eyes and the tamarisk-arrow method.

Snāuuiδka.note: Kərəsāspa kills the young rebel before he can enslave the two Spirits.

Soruš.note: Soruš reveals Kay Khosrow’s survival to Godarz, enabling his rescue.
Soruš later meets or summons the king before his disappearance.

Sorūš.note: Sorūš stops Fereydun from killing Zahhāk and orders his imprisonment.

Soʿdā.note: Masʿudi makes the Yemenite princess Soʿdā Kavus's consort and Siyavash's mother.

Spandārmad.myth: Preparation of the special bow and arrow
Spandārmad.note: Spandārmad directs or authorizes preparation of Arash’s extraordinary weapon.

Spəṇta Mainiiu.note: Kərəsāspa prevents Snāuuiδka from harnessing Spəṇta Mainiiu to his chariot.

Srid.note: Kavus orders Srid to kill the prophetic bull, then denies his remorseful death request.

Srvara.note: Kərəsāspa cooks unknowingly upon the serpent, then kills it after it rises.

Srōš.note: Srōš repeatedly calls Karsāsp from supernatural sleep to face Dahāg.
Srōš brings Karsāsp toward profession of the Zoroastrian religion.

Sudabeh.note: Ṭabarī alone identifies Sudabeh as Afrasiyab’s daughter.
Sudabeh becomes Kavus's wife and shares his imprisonment in Hamavaran.
Kavus condemns Sudabeh after her fraud is exposed but pardons her at Siyavash's request.
Siyavash’s stepmother propositions him, but he refuses her sexual advances.
Sudabeh falsely accuses Siyavash and fabricates evidence using aborted twins.
Siyavash intercedes when Kavus proposes executing Sudabeh, securing her pardon.

Sudāba.note: Rostam kills Sudāba after Siāvash’s death.

Sām.note: Middle Persian sources compound or identify Karsāsp with Sām.
New Persian genealogies place Sām among Garšāsp’s descendants.
Sām exposes Zāl, repents, retrieves him, and restores him publicly.

Sīmorḡ.note: Summoned by Zāl, the bird prescribes the operation and treatment that save Rudabeh.

Sīndoḵt.myth: Negotiations for Zāl and Rudāba’s marriage
Sīndoḵt.note: Sīndoḵt negotiates with Zāl’s family to prevent war and secure marriage.

Sīāvaš.note: Sīāvaš belongs to the royal generation served by Zāl’s house.

Sōšāns.note: Kay Husrōy assists Sōšāns and facilitates resurrection and the Final Body.

Tahmina.note: Tahmina becomes Rostam’s mutually willing lover or wife and bears Sohrāb.

Tahmineh.note: Tahmineh bears and raises Sohrab in Samangan.
Tahmineh reveals that Rostam is Sohrab's father and warns him about Afrasiab.
Tahmineh gives Sohrab Rostam's arm-token as proof of his descent.

Tahmuras.note: Some storyteller recensions associate Tahmuras with the revelation of Fereydun to Kaveh.

Tezhav.note: Bīžan defeats Tezhav’s side and captures Espanuy from his household.

The sorceress.note: The supernatural opponent approaches Esfandiyar disguised as a beautiful woman.
Esfandiyar exposes her with a sacred talisman, binds her, and kills her.

Tur.note: Afrasiyab descends from Tur, eponymous ancestral founder of Turan.
Fereydun grants Tur Turan, China, and the eastern lands.

Tus.note: Tus repeatedly commands Iranian armies against Afrasiyab and his relatives.
Bīžan campaigns under or alongside the Iranian commander Tus.
Bīžan and Tus share the fatal return after Kay Khosrow’s disappearance.
Tus commands under Kavus, receives his execution order, and champions Fariborz's succession.
Tusa appears as Haosrauuah’s ally in the heroic tradition.
Tus commands the Iranian army but disobeys Kay Khosrow’s route order.
Kay Khosrow punishes or threatens Tus after his disobedience causes Forud’s death.
Tus accompanies the king after warnings and dies in the snowstorm.
Tus is Rostam’s Iranian colleague despite frequent strategic disagreements.
Tus finds Siyavash’s future mother and later replaces Siyavash in command.
Tus participates among the Iranian commanders confronting Sohrab's invasion.

Tush.note: Tush is named as Esfandiyar's son in variant epic genealogies.

Tūs.note: Tūs urges Karsāsp to praise the Gāthās and Righteousness.

Uruuāxšaiia.note: Uruuāxšaiia is Kərəsāspa’s brother and the victim he avenges.

Vafra Navāza.note: Fereydun hurls or transforms Vafra Navāza into a bird.

Varəšava son of Dāna.note: Kərəsāspa kills Varəšava, son of Dāna.

Vayu.note: Vayu receives Kərəsāspa’s sacrifice and grants his requested victories.

Vaēsaka and his brood.note: Their heroic line forms part of the Turanian opposition to his forces.

Vištāspa.note: Esfandiyar is the son and designated successor of Vištāspa.
They are linked through the same weapon and later restoration traditions.

Vāyu.note: Vāyu receives Fereydun’s request and grants victory over Dahāka.
Haosrauuah sacrifices to Vāyu for divine assistance.
Wāy transports him and participates in his passage to immortality.

Vərəθraγna.note: Kavus's aerial travel is uncertainly associated with the deity's bird-form imagery.

Wesfāfarid.note: Ṭabari names Wesfāfarid as Kay Khosrow’s mother.
Wesfāfarid.source: Ṭabari, History of Prophets and Kings

White Div.note: The White Div blinds and imprisons Kavus before Rostam kills it.
Rostam kills White Div and uses his liver’s blood to cure blindness.

White Elephant.note: The young Rostam kills Sām’s white elephant with a mace.

Wind.note: A demonically deceived Wind attacks Karsāsp and threatens the earth.
Karsāsp persuades Wind to resume sustaining heaven and earth.

Wēw.note: Wēw and Karsāsp are jointly listed among sleepers or Renovation-makers.

Wīdrafš.note: Daqiqi says Esfandiyar kills Zarer's slayer; the Ayādgār credits Bastwar.

Xnąθaitī.note: The hostile pairikā is obscurely associated with Kərəsāspa.
Pahlavi exegesis treats Xnąθaitī as witch-desire leading Karsāsp into idolatry.

Zainigav.note: Afrasiyab defeats Zainigav after the Iranians request his assistance.

Zanga-ye Shavaran.note: Zanga returns Afrasiyab’s hostages and peace gifts on Siyavash’s behalf.

Zangeh-ye Shāvarān.note: Zangeh-ye Shāvarān joins Rostam’s party and participates in operations around Bīžan’s rescue.

Zar Bānu.note: Zar Bānu is Rostam’s daughter in later vengeance traditions.

Zar Bānū.note: Zar Bānū is Rostam’s daughter and Zāl’s granddaughter.
She accompanies Bānū Gošasp and Zāl during Bahman’s invasion.

Zarathustra.note: Afrasiyab ranges through seven regions trying unsuccessfully to seize Zarathustra’s glory.
Esfandiyar accepts the duty of defending and spreading Zarathustra's religion.
Later tradition says Zoroaster grants Esfandiyar bodily invulnerability.
A Zoroaster-derived sacred talisman exposes and binds the disguised sorceress.
Zarathustra defends Karsāsp’s deeds and promises to care for Fire.

Zardušt.note: Later eschatology assigns them distinct roles in restoring righteous rule and religion.
Suhrawardi presents both as recipients of divine or Kayanian illumination.

Zarer.note: Zarer is Esfandiyar's uncle and fellow champion of the religion.
Esfandiyar assumes command after Zarer's death and continues the religious war.

Zav.note: Zav expels or succeeds Afrasiyab, restoring rain, fertility and political order.
Zāl and the Iranian nobles select the aged Zav as king.

Zav son of Tahmāsp.note: Thaʿālibī relocates Arash’s episode to Zav’s reign without personal dialogue.

Zavara.note: Rostam's brother fights Esfandiyar's forces and kills his son Nush-Azar.

Zavareh.note: Zavareh, Rostam's brother, is Sohrab's paternal uncle.

Zavāra.note: Zavāra accompanies Rostam and attacks Esfandiyār’s camp.
Zavāra dies alongside Rostam during the Kabul ambush.
Zavāra is Zāl’s son and Rostam’s lieutenant.

Zhendeh-Razm.note: Zhendeh-Razm accompanies Sohrab because he can identify Rostam.

Zēnīgāw.note: Zēnīgāw attacks Iran during Kavus's reign in the older captivity complex.

pairikās.note: Many pairikās accompany Pitaona when Kərəsāspa attacks him.

the divs.note: Kavus forces the divs to construct crystal and gold palaces for him.

the sons of Viseh.note: The sons of Viseh serve as Turanian warriors under Afrasiyab.

Ābtin.note: Developed Persian tradition names Ābtin as Fereydun’s father.

Ādur Burzēn-Mihr.note: Esfandiyar receives or holds the sacred fire without being burned.

Ādur Gušnasp.myth: Destruction of Lake Čēčast idol temple
Ādur Gušnasp.note: The sacred fire rides or shines beside him during the temple’s destruction.

Ādur-tirs.note: The Bundahišn names Ādur-tirs as a son of Esfandiyar.

Āxrūra.note: Āxrūra is Haosrauuah’s son; both of their fravašis are venerated.

Āxrūrag.note: Āxrūrag appears as Karsāsp’s friend or helper against Gandarw.

Āθβiia.note: His Haoma pressing is rewarded with the birth of Θraētaona.

Āḏarnuš.note: Āḏarnuš is killed by Rostam’s side during the duel’s wider conflict.

Ōšnar.note: Ōšnar serves as a learned minister and administrator during Kavus's reign.

Šahriyār.note: Šahriyār is a later descendant of Borzū in Zāl’s lineage.

Šaḡād.note: Šaḡād is Zāl’s son by an unnamed Kabul slave woman.

Θrita.note: Θrita’s Haoma sacrifice produces Kərəsāspa and Uruuāxšaiia.

Ṭus.note: Zāl rejects Ṭus as unsuitable to succeed Nowḏar.
